name: Protecting Material Non-Public Information
title: Protecting Material Non-Public Information
answer: Protecting material non-public information (MNPI) is the set of controls, policies, and cultural practices that keep confidential corporate information from being misused in securities trading or other decisions. In an AI context, it covers data used to train or prompt models, model outputs that may reveal sensitive facts, and the use of AI tools to analyze filings, earnings, or deal pipelines. It also covers the fiduciary duty of directors, officers, and employees who hold MNPI and the compliance function that monitors their activity. The topic overlaps with insider trading law, information barriers, and disclosure controls, but it is broader than any single rule. The site's 219 compliance and regulation pages reflect how often these controls appear in rulemaking and enforcement.

sections.body: Protecting material non-public information (MNPI) is the set of controls, policies, and cultural practices that keep confidential corporate information from being misused in securities trading or other decisions. In an AI context, it covers data used to train or prompt models, model outputs that may reveal sensitive facts, and the use of AI tools to analyze filings, earnings, or deal pipelines. It also covers the fiduciary duty of directors, officers, and employees who hold MNPI and the compliance function that monitors their activity. The topic overlaps with insider trading law, information barriers, and disclosure controls, but it is broader than any single rule. The site's 219 compliance and regulation pages reflect how often these controls appear in rulemaking and enforcement.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The infrastructure for protecting MNPI runs on data classification, identity and access management, and logging systems that record who touched which file and when. Information barriers are enforced through permission groups, ethical walls, and separate deal rooms, often with need-to-know access. Surveillance platforms ingest email, chat, and trade data to flag patterns such as trading ahead of announcements. AI tools may be used to summarize documents or detect anomalies, but they need to run inside the same access controls as the underlying data. The site's 732 AI tools vary in whether they offer the audit trails and data residency controls that compliance teams require.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done through a lifecycle: classify information, restrict access, monitor use, and investigate exceptions. Compliance teams maintain restricted lists, watch lists, and wall-crossing procedures, and they require pre-clearance for trades by certain employees. When AI is used, teams review training data, prompts, and outputs for MNPI, and they log model interactions so that a later review can reconstruct what happened. Training and attestations remind staff of their duties, while surveillance and forensic reviews test whether the controls are working. Findings are escalated to legal, compliance, or the board depending on severity.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Protecting MNPI engages legal duties under securities law, fiduciary duties of loyalty and care, and contractual duties of confidentiality. The main risks are insider trading, tipping, misuse of deal information, and the leakage of confidential data through AI prompts or model training. Provenance matters because firms must know where data came from, who is allowed to see it, and whether an AI system has retained it. Audit trails, access logs, and model documentation are the evidence that support both defense and regulatory examination. The site's 354 merger and acquisition filings illustrate the volume of deal information that requires careful handling.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward more automated surveillance, tighter data provenance requirements, and clearer rules for generative AI in regulated workflows. Regulators are paying closer attention to how firms use AI to analyze confidential information and how they test those systems. Confidential computing, synthetic data, and local model deployment may reduce some leakage risks, but they also create new questions about auditability. The site's 117 listed AI-related instruments with daily prices are a reminder that governance failures can have market consequences.
